question.text: How should you set your mirrors, and how do you clear blind spots before changing lanes?

answer.text: Set the inside mirror to frame the whole back window and the side mirrors to barely show your vehicle; clear blind spots with a quick head turn and shoulder glance before lane changes and passes.

teaching.text: Mirrors first, then a quick head turn and shoulder glance before every lane change or pass. Remember: mirrors set, head turned.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Set the inside mirror to frame the whole back window and the side mirrors to barely show your vehicle; clear blind spots with a quick head turn and shoulder glance before lane changes and passes.

question.text: What should you do if you are riding in another driver's blind spot?

answer.text: Never linger in another driver's blind spot: speed up or drop back instead.

teaching.text: If you are in another driver's blind spot, speed up or drop back rather than staying there. Remember: speed up or drop back.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never linger in another driver's blind spot: speed up or drop back instead.

question.text: How do you handle your own blind spots compared with other drivers' blind spots?

answer.text: Your own blind spots need mirror setup plus head checks, while others' blind spots need you to speed up or drop back out.

teaching.text: Clear your own blind spots with mirrors and a head turn; leave other drivers' blind spots by speeding up or dropping back. Remember: check yours, leave theirs.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Your own blind spots need mirror setup plus head checks, while others' blind spots need you to speed up or drop back out.

question.text: Who counts as a vulnerable road user, and what does the law expect of drivers around them?

answer.text: Vulnerable users cover pedestrians, bicyclists, wheelchair, skateboard, skate, and scooter users, animals, and animal-drawn vehicles; distracted or careless driving around them is illegal, and you must drive to cover their mistakes.

teaching.text: Walkers, riders of all kinds, animals and animal-drawn vehicles are vulnerable users, and you drive to cover their mistakes. Remember: cover their mistakes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Vulnerable users cover pedestrians, bicyclists, wheelchair, skateboard, skate, and scooter users, animals, and animal-drawn vehicles; distracted or careless driving around them is illegal, and you must drive to cover their mistakes.

question.text: How should you guard pedestrians near schools, playgrounds, homes and crosswalks?

answer.text: Guard pedestrians near schools, playgrounds, and homes; let them fully cross before you turn; never pass at a crosswalk; stop and stay stopped until they clear your stopped lane.

teaching.text: Let pedestrians fully cross before you turn, and never pass at a crosswalk. Remember: let them fully cross.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Guard pedestrians near schools, playgrounds, and homes; let them fully cross before you turn; never pass at a crosswalk; stop and stay stopped until they clear your stopped lane.

question.text: For whom must you come to a full stop, and what is the penalty for failing and causing serious injury?

answer.text: Come to a full stop for cane or guide-dog users and for any pedestrian lawfully crossing; failing to stop and causing serious injury or death brings a Class one misdemeanor.

teaching.text: Cane, guide-dog and lawful crossings require a full stop, and failing to stop can bring a Class one misdemeanor. Remember: cane or dog, full stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Come to a full stop for cane or guide-dog users and for any pedestrian lawfully crossing; failing to stop and causing serious injury or death brings a Class one misdemeanor.

question.text: How do turning yields to pedestrians differ from the required full stops?

answer.text: Turning drivers wait out full crossings, while cane, guide-dog, and lawful crossings demand full stops backed by a Class one misdemeanor.

teaching.text: Turning drivers wait out the crossing; cane, guide-dog and lawful crossings need a full stop. Remember: wait out, or stop.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Turning drivers wait out full crossings, while cane, guide-dog, and lawful crossings demand full stops backed by a Class one misdemeanor.

question.text: What rights do bicyclists have on Virginia roads?

answer.text: Bicyclists share motor-vehicle right-of-way, may hold the lane center when needed for left turns or narrow lanes, ride all public roads except interstates and most freeways, and may approach from either direction on sidewalks, paths, and two-way bike lanes.

teaching.text: Bicyclists may take the lane center when needed and ride every public road except interstates and most freeways. Remember: bikes share the road.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bicyclists share motor-vehicle right-of-way, may hold the lane center when needed for left turns or narrow lanes, ride all public roads except interstates and most freeways, and may approach from either direction on sidewalks, paths, and two-way bike lanes.

question.text: How much clearance must you give when passing a cyclist, and may you use a bike lane to pass?

answer.text: Pass cyclists with at least three feet of clearance, changing lanes where the lane cannot spare it; motor vehicles may never use marked bike lanes, even to pass.

teaching.text: Give at least three feet when passing a cyclist, and never drive in a marked bike lane. Remember: three feet, never bike lane.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Pass cyclists with at least three feet of clearance, changing lanes where the lane cannot spare it; motor vehicles may never use marked bike lanes, even to pass.

question.text: How do bicyclists' rights differ from what drivers owe them?

answer.text: Bicyclists may take the lane center and most roads, while drivers owe them three feet, lane changes, and empty bike lanes.

teaching.text: Cyclists may use the lane; drivers owe three feet and empty bike lanes. Remember: lane center, three feet.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bicyclists may take the lane center and most roads, while drivers owe them three feet, lane changes, and empty bike lanes.

question.text: When should you check for bicycles, and why?

answer.text: Bicycles slip easily into blind spots: check for them before pull-outs, lane changes, turns, backing, door openings, and intersections, give room, and expect sudden stops.

teaching.text: Bikes slip into blind spots, so check for them before pull-outs, turns, backing, doors and intersections. Remember: bikes hide in blind spots.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bicycles slip easily into blind spots: check for them before pull-outs, lane changes, turns, backing, door openings, and intersections, give room, and expect sudden stops.

question.text: Why should you look twice for motorcycles?

answer.text: Look twice for motorcycles, since drivers expect four-wheelers and miss bikes until too late in over half of car-motorcycle crashes; check blind spots before every maneuver.

teaching.text: Drivers expect four-wheelers, so a second look is what catches the motorcycle. Remember: look twice, save lives.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Look twice for motorcycles, since drivers expect four-wheelers and miss bikes until too late in over half of car-motorcycle crashes; check blind spots before every maneuver.

question.text: How do the checks for bicycles differ from the looks for motorcycles?

answer.text: Bikes need checks at six maneuver points for their slipperiness, while motorcycles need double looks for their invisibility.

teaching.text: Check for bikes at each maneuver; look twice for motorcycles. Remember: check bikes, double-look motorcycles.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Bikes need checks at six maneuver points for their slipperiness, while motorcycles need double looks for their invisibility.

question.text: How should you follow a motorcycle?

answer.text: Never tailgate or lane-share with a motorcycle: add an extra second of following distance, double it in bad weather, expect sudden in-lane moves, and yield with double looks since bike speed and distance deceive.

teaching.text: Add an extra second behind a motorcycle, double it in bad weather, and never tailgate or lane-share. Remember: extra second behind bikes.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Never tailgate or lane-share with a motorcycle: add an extra second of following distance, double it in bad weather, expect sudden in-lane moves, and yield with double looks since bike speed and distance deceive.

question.text: What following rules apply behind a motorcycle?

answer.text: Motorcycles gain an extra following second doubled in weather, plus bans on tailgating and lane sharing.

teaching.text: An extra second behind motorcycles, doubled when the weather is bad. Remember: extra second, doubled wet.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Motorcycles gain an extra following second doubled in weather, plus bans on tailgating and lane sharing.

question.text: How should you drive around Norfolk light rail, The Tide?

answer.text: Around Norfolk light rail The Tide, with twenty-seven crossings over seven point four miles, expect trains on any track at any time, never circle lowered gates or stop, pass, or shift on tracks, look both ways before turning across, and cross only with room to clear fully.

teaching.text: Expect a train on any track at any time, and never stop on the tracks. Remember: trains anytime, any track.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Around Norfolk light rail The Tide, with twenty-seven crossings over seven point four miles, expect trains on any track at any time, never circle lowered gates or stop, pass, or shift on tracks, look both ways before turning across, and cross only with room to clear fully.

question.text: What does light rail forbid, and what does it demand?

answer.text: Light rail forbids circling gates and stopping on tracks, while demanding train expectation, double looks, and full clearance.

teaching.text: Never circle gates or stop on tracks; always expect trains and leave room to clear. Remember: never on the tracks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Light rail forbids circling gates and stopping on tracks, while demanding train expectation, double looks, and full clearance.

question.text: How fast do low-speed vehicles go, where may they run, and do golf carts qualify?

answer.text: Low-speed vehicles top out at twenty-one to twenty-five miles per hour and may run only on roads posted thirty-five miles per hour or less for licensed drivers or supervised permit holders, meeting federal safety plus Virginia registration and insurance rules; golf carts do not qualify.

teaching.text: Low-speed vehicles stay on roads posted thirty-five or less, and golf carts are not low-speed vehicles. Remember: thirty-five or less roads.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Low-speed vehicles top out at twenty-one to twenty-five miles per hour and may run only on roads posted thirty-five miles per hour or less for licensed drivers or supervised permit holders, meeting federal safety plus Virginia registration and insurance rules; golf carts do not qualify.

question.text: How do low-speed vehicles differ from golf carts?

answer.text: Low-speed vehicles run twenty-one to twenty-five on roads of thirty-five or less, while golf carts are not low-speed vehicles at all.

teaching.text: Low-speed vehicles have road and speed limits; golf carts are not in that group. Remember: golf carts do not qualify.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Low-speed vehicles run twenty-one to twenty-five on roads of thirty-five or less, while golf carts are not low-speed vehicles at all.

question.text: How do trucks, buses and RVs differ from cars, and what are their danger areas called?

answer.text: Trucks, tractor-trailers, buses, and RVs run longer, higher, and wider with slow acceleration and long stopping and turning needs; their danger areas are called No-Zones on the sides, front, and rear.

teaching.text: Large vehicles need long distances to stop and turn, and their danger areas are the No-Zones. Remember: big vehicles, No-Zones.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Trucks, tractor-trailers, buses, and RVs run longer, higher, and wider with slow acceleration and long stopping and turning needs; their danger areas are called No-Zones on the sides, front, and rear.

question.text: How do side No-Zones work on trucks, buses and RVs?

answer.text: Side No-Zones on trucks, buses, and RVs dwarf car blind spots because of wide turns: if you cannot see the driver's face in his mirror, he cannot see you.

teaching.text: If you cannot see the driver's face in the mirror, the driver cannot see you. Remember: no face, no see.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Side No-Zones on trucks, buses, and RVs dwarf car blind spots because of wide turns: if you cannot see the driver's face in his mirror, he cannot see you.

question.text: What is the danger of riding in a truck's rear No-Zone?

answer.text: Rear No-Zones hide your car from the truck driver and hide ahead traffic from you, leaving no escape at sudden stops; always hold a safe following distance.

teaching.text: Behind a truck you are hidden and cannot see ahead, so keep a safe following distance. Remember: no escape behind trucks.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Rear No-Zones hide your car from the truck driver and hide ahead traffic from you, leaving no escape at sudden stops; always hold a safe following distance.

question.text: What should you do after passing a truck, and why?

answer.text: Front No-Zones punish cutting in too soon or slowing after passing, since trucks need nearly twice car stopping time and room; combinations run up to sixty-five feet and may need over half a mile to pass, so return only with the whole truck front in your mirror and hold speed.

teaching.text: After passing, wait for the whole truck front in your mirror and hold your speed. Remember: whole truck in mirror.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Front No-Zones punish cutting in too soon or slowing after passing, since trucks need nearly twice car stopping time and room; combinations run up to sixty-five feet and may need over half a mile to pass, so return only with the whole truck front in your mirror and hold speed.

question.text: How do the side, rear and front No-Zones each put you at risk?

answer.text: Side zones hide you beside wide-turning trucks, rear zones hide you behind sudden stoppers, and front zones punish early cut-ins.

teaching.text: Side hides you, rear traps you, front punishes early cut-ins. Remember: side, rear, front.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Side zones hide you beside wide-turning trucks, rear zones hide you behind sudden stoppers, and front zones punish early cut-ins.

question.text: How do trucks, buses and RVs turn, and what must you never do?

answer.text: Trucks, buses, and RVs swing wide to turn with blind spots up to twenty feet ahead of the cab and about two hundred feet behind; never squeeze between them and the curb or another vehicle.

teaching.text: Turning trucks swing wide, so never squeeze between them and the curb or another vehicle. Remember: never squeeze beside turns.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Trucks, buses, and RVs swing wide to turn with blind spots up to twenty feet ahead of the cab and about two hundred feet behind; never squeeze between them and the curb or another vehicle.

question.text: How does returning after passing a truck differ from dealing with a turning truck?

answer.text: Passing returns need the whole truck front in the mirror at steady speed, while turning trucks forbid squeezing past at all.

teaching.text: Return steadily after the whole truck front shows; never squeeze past a turning truck. Remember: steady return, no squeeze.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Passing returns need the whole truck front in the mirror at steady speed, while turning trucks forbid squeezing past at all.

question.text: What does towing a light or medium trailer require and change?

answer.text: Light and medium trailers ride on safety chains and hitches with large mirrors needed; towing doubles passing, stopping, accelerating, and turning effort, and No-Zones apply.

teaching.text: Towing doubles the effort of every maneuver, and No-Zones apply to trailers too. Remember: towing doubles effort.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Light and medium trailers ride on safety chains and hitches with large mirrors needed; towing doubles passing, stopping, accelerating, and turning effort, and No-Zones apply.

question.text: How does towing a trailer compare with a truck's stopping demand?

answer.text: Trailers double every maneuver's effort, matching trucks' near-double stopping demand.

teaching.text: A trailer doubles your effort, much like a truck needs nearly double the stopping room. Remember: both nearly double.

audio_scripts.must_match_card_back: Trailers double every maneuver's effort, matching trucks' near-double stopping demand.
